questions.q: In Azure's resource hierarchy, what sits above subscriptions so that policy can be applied once and inherited downward?
questions.explain: Management groups group multiple subscriptions together so policy and access controls can be applied once, at the top, and inherit down to every subscription beneath them.

questions.q: What is AWS Organizations' equivalent of an Azure management group?
questions.explain: Organizational units (OUs) group AWS accounts the same way Azure management groups group subscriptions — a common pattern uses OUs like Security, Production, Non-Production, and Sandbox.

questions.q: What does AWS encourage that Azure doesn't push nearly as hard, according to this lesson?
options: One AWS account per workload or team, rather than grouping many workloads inside one subscription
Using a single AWS account for the entire company, no matter its size
Avoiding organizational units entirely in favor of a flat account structure
Treating resource groups as AWS's primary access-control boundary
questions.explain: The lesson notes that AWS actively encourages one account per workload or team as the hard billing/access boundary, whereas Azure tends to hold more inside a single subscription using resource groups.

questions.q: What are the four layers of the governance architecture model this course is organized around?
questions.explain: The lesson's four-layer model — identity (Chapter 2), policy (Chapter 4), data (Chapter 3), and monitoring — maps directly onto this course's chapter structure.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say "where does this live in the hierarchy" is often the first productive governance question for an ungoverned resource?
options: Because a resource's hierarchy placement determines what policy, logging, and cost ownership it inherits before anyone even checks its individual access controls
Because hierarchy placement is purely a cosmetic/organizational detail with no governance impact
Because individual resource permissions always override anything inherited from the hierarchy
Because the hierarchy only matters for billing, not for security or governance
questions.explain: A resource dropped into the wrong subscription or account inherits the wrong policy, logging configuration, and cost owner — so hierarchy placement is usually worth checking before diving into the resource's individual access controls.
